headlines.title: United flight returns to SFO after blowing tire during departure
headlines.description: A United Airlines flight returned safely to San Francisco International Airport Thursday after blowing a tire during departure, the FAA said. United Flight 1189, a Boeing 737-800 bound for Los Cabos International Airport in Mexico, landed back at SFO at about 11:45 a.m., according to the FAA. Footage from NBC Bay Area SkyRanger showed people exiting the plane via stairs – while the aircraft was still on the tarmac – and getting onto buses to return to the terminal. The plane was carrying 165 passengers and eight crew members, United said. No injuries were reported. United said it arraigned for a different plane to take the passengers to Los Cabos later Thursday afternoon. The FAA said it will conduct an investigation.

headlines.title: Children under 10 crash car into pedestrian in Oakland, sending woman to hospital
headlines.description: Two children under the age of 10 took a car belonging to one of their parents Thursday and later struck a pedestrian in Oakland, leaving her in critical condition, police said. The collision happened at about 9:30 a.m. in the area of 35th and Mangels avenues, not far from Interstate 580, according to police. Police said the pedestrian, a woman in her 30s, was taken to a hospital. The two children, who sources said are 6 and 4 years old, were also taken to a hospital and listed in stable condition. Witness Anthony Hudson said multiple people ran to help the woman, performing CPR until paramedics arrived. “It was just tragic,” Hudson said. The kids appeared to be traveling northbound on 35th Avenue when they hit another vehicle traveling in the opposite direction, causing them to lose control and hit the pedestrian as she was walking with a dog in a crosswalk, according to police. Witnesses said the dog appeared to be OK. Witnesses, shocked at the ages of the children in the car, said the kids were lying on the ground with injuries and appeared to be in shock after the crash. The parents of the children were cooperating with the investigation. It wasn’t immediately known if alcohol and/or drugs played a role, police said. An investigation is ongoing. Oakland 17 hours ago Oakland Aug 2 Oakland Aug 1

headlines.title: Arrest made in 6-alarm fire at Foster City condominium complex
headlines.description: A Foster City resident was arrested in connection with a six-alarm blaze that ripped through a condominium complex and left four firefighters injured last weekend, police said Thursday. Keith Tompkins was arrested for unlawfully causing a fire resulting in injury to firefighters; obstructing and delaying a police investigation; and willfully resisting, obstructing, or delaying a fire investigation, according to police. The blaze at the Spinnaker Cove condominium complex at 815 Sea Spray Ln. sparked Sunday afternoon and raged for several hours. Four firefighters were injured but are expected to be OK. Everyone was rescued, but the flames spread across roughly 50 units in the building, which was built in the 1980s and, according to residents, had no sprinklers. Investigators determined the blaze was caused by an unattended gas grill on an exterior balcony. Tompkins was taken into custody without incident and booked into the San Mateo County Jail, police said. He later posted bond and was released on Wednesday. In a phone call with Tompkins on Thursday, he told NBC Bay Area that things are difficult right now, adding that he wasn’t sure if he should talk. Tompkins previously spoke to NBC Bay Area a few times outside the burned condos. Prosecutors on Thursday said they didn’t have the case file yet, but the district attorney confirmed the arrest and will wait while the police investigation continues. Foster City Aug 3 Foster City Aug 2 4 firefighters injured in six-alarm fire at Foster City condominium complex

headlines.title: Pedestrian killed in collision on southbound Highway 85 in San Jose
headlines.description: A pedestrian was killed early Thursday morning after being struck by a vehicle on southbound Highway 85 in San Jose, according to the California Highway Patrol. The crash was reported shortly after 1:30 a.m. near the Camden Avenue off-ramp. Patrol officers temporarily stopped all southbound traffic and diverted vehicles onto the Camden Avenue off-ramp. It was later reopened, and all lanes were back open by 3:50 a.m., according to the CHP. No further information about the crash was immediately available

headlines.title: Annual Silicon Valley Pain Index findings released
headlines.description: Researchers at San Jose State University on Thursday revealed this year’s index on economic inequality in Silicon Valley. The Silicon Valley Pain Index, a report put together by SJSU’s Human Rights Institute, evaluates societal needs such as housing, food and childcare. The goal is to inform government, community leaders and the public of persistent inequalities in areas including employment, education, housing, population, health and overall well-being. The index shows that the top 10% of residents hold 75% of the area’s wealth. The bottom 50% of residents hold less than 1%. “We have an even greater gap in income between the wealthiest and the rest of us,” lead author Anji Buckner-Capone said. “We have seen more schools close. We have seen increases in compromised physical and mental health. We have far too many individuals and families who are unsure how they will make ends meet.” According to the index, San Jose ranks as one of the most expensive large cities in the United States. To buy a standard home, citizens need an income of over $460,000. “We have abundant resources,” The Health Trust CEO Dr. Tony Iton said. “There’s enough for everybody to get food and healthcare and childcare. It’s not like there are shortages of these things. It’s just the policy is not investing in our people.”

headlines.title: Vogue World to be hosted in San Francisco in 2027
headlines.description: Vogue announced Thursday that its global fashion and cultural event, Vogue World, will be hosted in San Francisco next year. “Vogue believes in celebrating cities, and San Francisco is a city like none other,” said Anna Wintour in a statement. Wintour is the chief content officer of Vogue’s publisher Conde Nast, and the global editorial director of Vogue. “There’s a history of rebelliousness here, as well as incredible innovation,” Wintour added. “I love that San Francisco has always stood up for its values and the things it believes in. We think it’s the perfect setting for Vogue World 2027.” Vogue World is a one-day, annual event featuring high-end runway shows and musical performances. It focuses on local cultural themes, draws celebrity attendees, and includes donations to local charities. “Creativity and free expression have been the engine of San Francisco for generations, and that spirit will be on full display at Vogue World 2027,” said Mayor Daniel Lurie in a statement. Lurie said that bringing Vogue World to San Francisco will show that the city is “on the rise.” “Thanks to our ecosystem of talented designers, musicians, and small businesses — and the artists and workers behind them — visitors are coming to our city, and our economy is recovering,” he said. “Vogue World will support San Francisco’s creative minds and strengthen the entire ecosystem.” The event will be held in the fall of 2027. Vogue said that more information on the event will be coming.

headlines.title: Experts warn of high Bay Area flood risk during super El Niño
headlines.description: Thousands of viewers tuned in to a virtual town hall this week with climate experts providing insight into the possible impacts of a super El Nino event in the Bay Area and across the state. “We may be seeing an event that we haven’t really seen before in living memory in California,” said climate scientist Daniel Swain. “The impacts of that are something that’s really the focus of tonight’s conversation.” The town hall was hosted by state Sen. Mike McGuire, D-Healdsburg, and saw nearly 6,000 viewers online Tuesday. “This super El Nino has a real potential for larger and more destructive winter storms, significant flooding events, and ocean-based heat waves, which we’re already starting to see off the Pacific,” McGuire said. “At the end of the day, we can’t control the weather, but what we can control is how prepared we are before the weather hits.” El Nino is a temporary warming of the Eastern Tropical Pacific Ocean that can lead to significant climate events around the world. But this year’s El Nino is gearing up to be a super El Nino, which is the term used for an exceptionally strong El Nino event. That’s because the temperatures in the Eastern Tropical Pacific are reaching record-high numbers. “We’ve never seen ocean temperatures in the Eastern Tropical Pacific as warm as they are today in the region that matters for El Nino,” Swain said. On the Northern California coast and in the Bay Area, scientists are predicting an increased risk of flooding, heavy rainfall, high sea levels, a warm fall season, and lightning. “The fact that that we have these huge changes happening in the Pacific that could lead to more amplified, more active storm track could really impact the winter for Northern California and the Bay Area,” said Bay Area meteorologist Mark Tamayo. Speakers noted that if heavy rains do arrive, they will likely peak in December and January. Mark Merrifield, the director of the Scripps Center for Climate Change Impacts and Adaptation, said “we’re expecting likely the highest sea levels ever recorded on the California coast associated with this event.” Along with stronger rains and larger ocean waves, high sea levels could play into greater coastal flooding risk, which is already exacerbated by king tides that arrive in wintertime in Northern California. Merrifield noted that high sea levels will also cause water rising in the San Francisco Bay and even in the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta. “As the sea level rises along the open coast, it also raises the water level in the bays and harbors along the coast,” Merrifield said. The panel also warned of a greater probability of fires in the region due to lightning storms. “Those storms could destabilize the atmosphere enough to produce maybe some more thunderstorm potential and more fires,” Tamayo said. “It’s been hot, it’s been dry, and everything’s ready to burn. So if you add lightning to the mix, I am concerned.’ Nate Ortiz, the assistant director of planning and preparedness at the California Office of Emergency Management, provided some tips on how residents can start to get prepared for the possible El Nino impacts. He recommended signing up for local emergency alerts and creating a “go bag,” which is a kit containing essential survival items necessary to be self-sufficient for 72 hours. People should have cash in case ATM machines go down, have some pet food ready to go if needed, gather key documents like passports and social security cards, charge or fuel their cars, and keep mobile devices charged. “We’re going to be doing a lot of work to do our part,” Ortiz said. “But make sure that you’re doing your part to get those alerts and be able to sustain for a little while.” While the panel made a range of possible impacts associated with El Nino, the predictions are not guaranteed to happen. But with the current forecast and conditions in the Eastern Tropical Pacific, experts are raising the alarm as a precaution. “Our best predictive models are suggesting that this year’s event could significantly exceed the magnitude of any previously observed event in the modern era,” Swain said. “The whole reason we’re here is to think about what could happen, the potential risks that might entail, how we can better prepare for them in the short-run, and also how it might prepare us more for the future.”

headlines.title: Faith leaders hold vigil in SF for people killed in immigration detention, raids
headlines.description: About 100 people gathered outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement field office in San Francisco on Wednesday for a vigil to honor the people who have died in immigration raids and detention. “Together today we will cultivate a sacred space to grieve and mourn the horrendous violence of the U.S. detention and immigration enforcement systems,” said organizer and Buddhist practitioner Sophie Dipti Sarkar at the event. A group of local leaders from a range of faiths led songs, prayers, and offerings to recognize the people who have been fatally shot during ICE raids or died in immigration detention since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term, which has seen a rise in immigration enforcement and deportations. So far this year, at least 24 people have died in ICE custody, according to the National Immigration Project, an organization that advocates and litigates for immigrants. “We are here today because we refuse to stand by and watch as our neighbors, community members, and family members are kidnapped from their schools, workplaces, homes, airports, or while driving their children to daycare or school,” said Rabbi Cat Zavis from the Beyt Tikkun synagogue in Oakland during a speech. Photos of people who died during ICE raids or in detention were strung together along the fencing in front of the field office. A table covered in fake candles and butterflies stood as a centerpiece of the vigil. One by one, the group collectively spoke the names of each of the deceased while tying paper flowers to the fencing. “We are here today because every person is more than a number,” Zavis said. The vigil was followed by a march through downtown to the office of U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla, D-California, a couple of blocks away. The group held another rally outside the office with speakers urging for Padilla to fight for contact visitation between family and friends of those in ICE custody at the California City Detention Facility, located in Kern County. Family and friends are allowed to visit loved ones at the facility, but all visits are non-contact, meaning that visitors can only see detainees through glass. Samantha Sanchez Tayson, a pregnant mother whose husband is in custody at the California City Detention Facility, talked about the impacts of her husband not being able to physically be with his family. “He’s in a depressed place, and he doesn’t see us, and he can’t hug us,” she said. “That’s why my children and I are here to ask for help from the senator to see if he can find a way to get the glass out between us for the visits.” Members of California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice, an organization that provides legal services for those in immigration detention, presented a petition to some of Padilla’s staff. The public petition demanding to allow contact visitation at California City Detention Facility included about 1,100 signatures. The crowd chanted “Hugs beyond bars now” as it handed over the signatures to Padilla’s staff.

headlines.title: California Prop 1: Voters to decide on affordable housing bond measure
headlines.description: With the November midterm election coming up, California voters will have several propositions to consider in addition to candidates. Fourteen new propositions, ranging from the environment to taxes, will be on the ballot. Proposition 1 attempts to address affordable housing. Housing Trust Silicon Valley said half of renters are spending more than 30% of their income on rent. “It’s a huge crisis, and statewide as well,” Housing Trust Silicon Valley CFO Julie Mahowald said. “There are over a million households, people struggling to find affordable housing in the state.” Bipartisan state lawmakers put Prop 1 on the ballot to address the issue. “Prop 1 is an affordable housing bond, $11 billion affordable housing bond,” NBC Bay Area political contributor Guy Marzorati said. “The state would issue these bonds and then make it easier basically to finance construction. The idea here is there’s not enough affordable housing in the state, there’s not enough supply. This would help with that.” Marzaroti said Prop 1 is a bond measure, not a direct tax on individuals. “Really what it means is that the state will have to repay those bonds over the years from the state general fund,” he said. “That’s a little bit different from how veteran bonds are treated in here in Proposition 1. Those would be repaid by the actual homeowner.” If passed, the state would issue grants and low interest loans to local jurisdictions and private developers. Housing Trust Silicon Valley said Prop 1 would be a huge shot in the arm for working families, with thousands of affordable housing units ready to go up as soon as the measure passes. “They’re ready to put shovels in the ground, but we need this money,” Mahowald said. “To have 40,000 ready now means that when these funds are approved, there’ll be housing available to our neighbors more quickly.” Others such as the Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association question the financial element of the proposition. “If this is important, why isn’t it in the state budget?” Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association President Mark Hinkle said. “You have to think about it. The state legislators put this on the ballot. Why didn’t they put it in the budget? Clearly it’s not important to them.” The association said a time of state budget deficits is not a time to get into more debt. “Bonds are the equivalent to a mortgage,” Hinkle said. “What do we know about mortgages? By the time you actually pay it off, it’s double the cost.” Prop 1 includes $1 billion for veterans’ housing assistance. Voters will decide on the measure on Nov. 3.

headlines.title: 19 displaced, 18 rescued after 2-alarm fire in SF's Western Addition
headlines.description: 19 residents were displaced and 18 people were rescued after a two-alarm apartment fire tore through San Francisco’s Western Addition early Thursday morning, fire officials said. The fire was reported at about 1:56 a.m. in the 800 block of Fillmore Street. The San Francisco Fire Department initially placed the fire’s location in the 900 block. Firefighters found heavy fire in a three-story, multi-unit residential building over commercial space with multiple occupants in need of rescue. The blaze quickly escalated to a two-alarm response. Crews rescued 18 people from second- and third-floor windows using ground and aerial ladders, while several other residents were rescued from inside the building, according to the department. One civilian was injured and is expected to recover. The fire spread to two structures — 865 Fillmore St. and 855 Fillmore St. — but firefighters prevented it from extending to surrounding buildings. The fire was contained at 3:25 a.m. and declared under control at 3:33 a.m. The San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency provided a bus to serve as a temporary shelter for displaced residents while the San Francisco Human Services Agency and the American Red Cross provided emergency assistance and shelter information. Firefighters remained at the scene Thursday morning extinguishing hot spots and investigating the cause of the fire, which remains under investigation. Authorities urged the public to continue avoiding the area around Fillmore and Fulton streets, as well as nearby Grove Street, while crews cleared the scene.

headlines.title: Greg Papa laid off by Bay Area sports radio station KNBR
headlines.description: Bay Area sports radio station KNBR has laid off legendary sportscaster Greg Papa. Papa hosted the “Papa & Silver” show with Greg Silver, who was also let go. Papa is a 42-year broadcasting veteran. The 63-year-old has been away from work as he battles cancer. He returned home last month after a life-threatening 78-day hospital stay that included lung failure. NBC Bay Area reached out to KNBR and Cumulus, the station’s owner, but did not immediately hear back. Papa still has his job as the San Francisco 49ers radio announcer, though he’s not excepted to call games this upcoming season.

headlines.title: San Jose Unified students start new school year after district reorganization
headlines.description: Thousands of students across the San Jose Unified School District are starting the school year at different campuses after the district reorganized schools because of declining enrollment. The changes follow months of emotional debate, with parents raising concerns about losing neighborhood schools and the communities built around them. District leaders said consolidating campuses will allow the district to offer stronger academic programs and provide more support for students. Over the summer, crews prepared campuses for the start of the school year by deep cleaning schools, making repairs and completing facility upgrades. NBC Bay Area’s Ali Reid has more in the video above.
